assessment.nobel_worthiness: The heterogeneous-firm framework changed how trade is modelled. It explains exporter selection, within-industry reallocation and a gains-from-trade channel that older models missed. It produced a large body of quantitative and empirical work and is now the standard workhorse in trade research and policy analysis.
assessment.attribution: Melitz (2003) is the central, widely recognised contribution. Helpman's work on firm heterogeneity with Melitz and Yeaple, together with his broader theory of trade and industrial organisation, makes him the natural co-recipient. Redding is a major contributor to quantitative extensions but is a later-stage, more incremental figure. Other contributors (Bernard, Jensen, Eaton, Kortum) are acknowledged but fall outside this candidate's credited names.
assessment.maturity: More than two decades of confirmation through firm-level datasets across many countries. The core predictions are well supported, and the framework has been integrated into policy and quantitative trade modelling. Trade has not been recognised since 2008, so timing is favourable.
uncertainties: Some committee members may prefer the broader Helpman-Grossman political-economy-of-trade strand (a separate ballot entry), or consider that the 2008 prize already covered new trade theory.
Proper attribution relative to Bernard-Jensen empirical priority and to Eaton-Kortum is debatable.
My assessment relies on background knowledge and was not independently verified.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The New Keynesian framework, built on nominal rigidities, staggered contracts and interest-rate rules, is the dominant paradigm for monetary policy analysis in central banks worldwide. It has had a very large practical effect on inflation targeting and policy design.
assessment.attribution: Taylor contributed staggered contracts and the Taylor rule, Calvo the time-dependent pricing model, and Woodford the systematic theoretical synthesis of policy. Gali, Gertler, Christiano, Eichenbaum, Smets and others made major contributions (estimated DSGE models, the New Keynesian Phillips curve). The pool of credited names is large, so a three-person cut is hard and omits important contributors.
assessment.maturity: Fully mature. Roughly four decades of influence, with tested successes and limits (for example the post-2021 inflation episode and the zero lower bound). The prize would come late relative to the original contributions.
uncertainties: Selecting three names from eight or more plausible contributors is contested and risks leaving out essential credit.
The framework's forecasting failures, and the recognition already given to earlier rational-expectations and macro-policy work, may lower committee enthusiasm.
I did not independently verify the relative priority of each contribution.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Kiyotaki-Moore (1997) shows how collateral constraints amplify and propagate shocks, creating credit cycles. It is a foundational mechanism for understanding financial crises and for macro-financial models, with large influence on research and policy after 2008.
assessment.attribution: Kiyotaki and Moore are the clear originators of the credit-cycle mechanism. Gertler and Gilchrist are important for the financial accelerator and empirical evidence, but Bernanke-Gertler work was partly covered by the 2022 prize on banks and financial crises, so I keep the proposal to the two originators.
assessment.maturity: Nearly three decades of citations and extensions into macroprudential and quantitative macro models. The 2022 prize recognised related financial-crisis work, which raises the question of overlap but also confirms the field's standing.
uncertainties: Overlap with the 2022 laureates' contributions may reduce the perceived novelty margin.
Empirical identification of collateral channels remains debated.
Whether Gertler should be included given the financial accelerator lineage is open.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The top-income and wealth-distribution series rebuilt the long-run empirical record of inequality from tax and historical data. They reshaped research and public debate across economics, economic history and policy. Strong methodological contribution through data construction, with theoretical and policy claims that are more contested.
assessment.attribution: Piketty and Saez started the top-incomes series (the 2003 QJE paper). Zucman's work on offshore wealth and distributional national accounts is an important extension but is more recent. Related long-run data efforts (Atkinson, now deceased, and others) complicate attribution.
assessment.maturity: Over two decades of data and confirmation across countries (World Inequality Database). The measurement contribution is well established. Theoretical claims on r>g and wealth taxation are less settled.
uncertainties: Debate over data methodology (for example the treatment of capital income and the US distributional accounts), and over the theoretical claims in Capital in the Twenty-First Century.
Policy and political salience may affect how the committee weighs the work.
Whether the committee weights the measurement contribution above the more contested theory.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The China-shock studies and the task-based approach to technology and labour demand transformed understanding of how trade and automation shape local labour markets, wage inequality and politics. The work combines credible empirical designs with a conceptual framework and has broad policy relevance.
assessment.attribution: Autor-Dorn-Hanson is the cohesive team behind the China-shock evidence. Autor also has a distinct earlier line with Levy and Murnane on tasks, and with Katz on skill premia. Acemoglu and Restrepo (task models) are outside this entry, and Acemoglu received the 2024 prize, which affects the overlap with the task-theory side.
assessment.maturity: About a decade of confirmation, with continuing debate over persistence, magnitudes and generalisation. The core empirical findings have been replicated and extended. Broad adoption, though still open to refinement.
uncertainties: Partial overlap with the 2024 laureates on technology and institutions, and with the 2021 prize on empirical methods.
Whether Katz should be included instead of Dorn for the long-run skill-premium strand.
Magnitude and persistence of the shock effects are still debated.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The Berry-Levinsohn-Pakes demand-estimation framework and Pakes's dynamic-model contributions made structural estimation of differentiated-product markets practical. They are now a core toolkit for merger analysis, antitrust and empirical industrial organisation, with substantial real-world application.
assessment.attribution: Pakes is the clearest central figure (dynamic games, Ericson-Pakes, BLP). Berry and Levinsohn are credited with BLP (1995). Bresnahan, Reiss, Benkard and Levin are important contributors to the wider field. A limit of three names omits significant contributors.
assessment.maturity: More than three decades of use. The methods are mature and standard, with well-known practical issues (for example identification and numerical computation).
uncertainties: Whether the committee judges the contribution to be primarily methodological and therefore of narrower impact than the other top-ranked entries.
Attribution among Bresnahan, Pakes, Berry and Levinsohn.
Background-knowledge assessment not independently verified.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Large administrative datasets were used to measure intergenerational mobility and its geographic variation, and then to study causal place and neighbourhood effects. The contribution is empirical and data-led, with direct relevance to policy on opportunity and inequality. Scale and credibility of the data are notable.
assessment.attribution: Chetty is the central figure, and Hendren the main collaborator on place-effects identification. Friedman and Katz contributed substantially to other strands. Chetty's other work (public economics, taxation, teacher value-added) is outside this entry and could make a separate case.
assessment.maturity: Roughly a decade of major results, with ongoing replication and extension. Credible and widely cited, but recent relative to the laureate norm. Open questions remain on causal interpretation of geographic differences.
uncertainties: Short time horizon relative to typical Nobel recognition.
Debate about identification of place effects and about statistical bias in some mobility measures.
Age and career stage of the nominees may favour waiting.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Models of present bias, self-control and reference-dependent preferences formalised psychologically grounded departures from standard theory, with applications in savings, consumption and policy design. The contribution is conceptually important, extending the behavioural-economics recognition given to Thaler in 2017 and Kahneman in 2002.
assessment.attribution: Rabin has contributions across behavioural theory (fairness, reference dependence, belief updating). Laibson is central for quasi-hyperbolic discounting and its empirical and policy applications. Koszegi (reference-dependent preferences) and O'Donoghue (present bias) are strong contributors who are outside my two-name proposal.
assessment.maturity: Decades of theory and growing but mixed field evidence. Some constructs (for example loss aversion magnitudes and replication of behavioural effects) are debated. Prior prizes cover part of the territory.
uncertainties: Overlap with the Kahneman and Thaler prizes may reduce marginal appetite.
Replication concerns and the debate over welfare analysis with behavioural agents.
Attribution among a large group of equally important behavioural theorists.
